title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and OpenFlow
source_scope: The full SDN guide, five source diagrams, examples, glossary, references, revision questions, and source qualifications are retained. evidence.section: 1.1 Core Definition and Architectural Shift

question_links.rationale: The two architectural properties separate control logic from forwarding across several switches; logical centralization can use physically distributed controller servers.

evidence.section: 1.1 Core Definition and Architectural Shift

question_links.rationale: The traditional per-router control processes are contrasted with a logically centralized controller platform, not with mandatory static rules or restrictions on Ethernet.

evidence.section: 1.1 Core Definition and Architectural Shift

question_links.rationale: The global network map and northbound programs define traffic-engineering policy for multiple forwarding devices. This supports programmatic policy changes, not an atomic-update or universal compatibility guarantee.

evidence.section: 3.2 The Network OS (NOS) and Control Programs
The Network OS (NOS)
The Control Program

question_links.rationale: The NOS maintains a network-wide graph/database with defined consistency and freshness. This enables global decisions without guaranteeing a perfectly current view, automatic loop freedom, or failure immunity.

evidence.section: 4.1 The `<Match, Action>` Primitive and Switch Flow Tables

question_links.rationale: Header matching selects a prioritized table entry and its actions; per-switch Dijkstra or random-port hashing is not the OpenFlow mechanism taught.

evidence.section: 4.3 Out-of-Band vs. In-Band SDN Control Planes

question_links.rationale: In-band controller messages share physical forwarding links with data; out-of-band uses a separate management path with deployment-dependent physical isolation.

evidence.section: 4.1 The `<Match, Action>` Primitive and Switch Flow Tables

question_links.rationale: Supported header fields and exact/wildcard matching give flexible match-action handling. The keyed arbitrary-fields phrase overstates the version- and hardware-dependent capability explicitly qualified in the guide.
question_links.review_note: Replace arbitrary packet header fields with supported match fields and masks; the version and switch capabilities limit what can be matched.

evidence.section: 3.2 The Network OS (NOS) and Control Programs
The Network OS (NOS)
The Control Program

question_links.rationale: The NOS collects distributed state into a global view; the hypervisor additionally presents virtual views. The benefit is a reusable abstraction, not a real-time or scalability guarantee.

evidence.section: 2.5 Motivating Case Study 2: Distributed Access Control Failure

question_links.rationale: The added backup path bypasses R5 while the old interface ACL stays in place. Correct SDN applications must update rule placement and order; SDN alone does not guarantee security.

evidence.section: 2.3 Why Traditional Networks Are Hard to Reason About and Evolve

question_links.rationale: An operator changes link metrics to induce a distributed protocol to choose a path instead of directly programming that path; interacting protocols complicate the outcome.

evidence.section: 4.1 The `<Match, Action>` Primitive and Switch Flow Tables

question_links.rationale: The action associated with supported header-field matches controls packet handling. The primitive neither synchronizes controller replicas nor restricts matching to IPv4/TCP.

evidence.section: 4.1 The `<Match, Action>` Primitive and Switch Flow Tables

question_links.rationale: The source action example combines header replacement/push/pop with forwarding to ports 5 and 6, directly supporting rewriting plus multiple output ports.

evidence.section: Translating Virtual Policies to Physical Rules

question_links.rationale: A hypervisor maps tenant virtual topologies and policies to physical enforcement rules while sharing infrastructure and preserving isolation.

evidence.section: 5.3 Practical and Algorithmic Challenges (4D / SDN)
3.2 The Network OS (NOS) and Control Programs
The Network OS (NOS)
The Control Program

question_links.rationale: The consistency challenge requires compatible replica decisions as the control platform scales. Required lesson 08 explains distributed state synchronization and message passing; coordinating that state adds communication work, a direct synthesis of the two sections.

evidence.section: 5.3 Practical and Algorithmic Challenges (4D / SDN)
3.1 Vertically Integrated Appliances vs. Open Horizontal SDN Stack

question_links.rationale: Interoperability with legacy routers/BGP is an explicit challenge. Required lesson 07 explains the exposed forwarding-interface and compatible-device boundary; lack of that interface can require integration. The key overgeneralizes traditional equipment as universally lacking OpenFlow.
question_links.review_note: Specify legacy devices without a compatible OpenFlow interface. Traditional equipment is not universally incapable of OpenFlow, and legacy/BGP interoperation is broader than protocol support alone.

evidence.section: 3.1 Vertically Integrated Appliances vs. Open Horizontal SDN Stack

question_links.rationale: An open interface to packet forwarding is an explicit component enabling separation from vendor control software. The history provides context rather than required additional mechanism.

evidence.section: 5.2 Why SDN Happened When It Did: Technical and Economic Drivers

question_links.rationale: Cloud scale, fine-grained programmability, merchant silicon, cost pressure, and the pragmatic use of existing switch tables explain adoption without mandating encryption or CPU quotas.

evidence.section: 5.2 Why SDN Happened When It Did: Technical and Economic Drivers

question_links.rationale: The source names network virtualization as the killer application: tenants define isolated topologies, address spaces, and policies on shared physical servers/switches.

evidence.section: Translating Virtual Policies to Physical Rules

question_links.rationale: The hypervisor translates a single virtual policy and topology into concrete physical enforcement configurations rather than scheduling CPU or assigning MACs by priority.

evidence.section: Where the Complexity Goes

question_links.rationale: The compiler analogy explicitly moves distributed systems complexity into reusable NOS and hypervisor code, simplifying application-specific control logic.

evidence.section: 4.2 Step-by-Step Execution Example: TCP Handshake and HTTP over OpenFlow
Two Ways the Controller Can Respond to a Table Miss (`Packet-IN`)

question_links.rationale: The example sends table misses to the controller only because a suitable miss rule is installed; the guide explicitly contrasts the OpenFlow 1.3 default drop when that rule is absent. The unconditional key needs that assumption.
question_links.review_note: State the configured miss-to-controller rule and OpenFlow version. Without that rule, OpenFlow 1.3 defaults to dropping unmatched packets; the controller outcome is not unconditional.

evidence.section: 4.1 The `<Match, Action>` Primitive and Switch Flow Tables

question_links.rationale: The source explicitly combines changing header fields with output to ports 5 and 6; the other options provide only one of modification and multi-output behavior.

evidence.section: 3.3 Forwarding Abstraction and Network Virtualization
Purpose of the Forwarding Abstraction

question_links.rationale: The ISA analogy and vendor-neutral forwarding interface let control programs specify forwarding state without binding to one hardware vendor, subject to advertised device capabilities.

evidence.section: Translating Virtual Policies to Physical Rules

question_links.rationale: The abstract view exposes a tenant-defined logical switch/topology while the physical network is shared. It does not promise address obfuscation, symmetric TCP paths, or IPv4/IPv6 conversion.

evidence.section: Translating Virtual Policies to Physical Rules
4.1 The `<Match, Action>` Primitive and Switch Flow Tables

question_links.rationale: The hypervisor translates virtual tenant policy into physical enforcement rules. Required lesson 12 identifies the corresponding match-action flow-table entries; policy placement need not install an identical rule on every switch.

evidence.section: 5.3 Practical and Algorithmic Challenges (4D / SDN)

question_links.rationale: Controller event load and flow-setup rate grow with thousands of switches and millions of flows, potentially bottlenecking centralized decision elements.

evidence.section: Two Ways the Controller Can Respond to a Table Miss (`Packet-IN`)
Complete End-to-End Sequence (Reactive `Flow-MOD` Mode)
5.3 Practical and Algorithmic Challenges (4D / SDN)

question_links.rationale: The guide discusses controller reliability and locally forwarding with still-valid rules, but does not specify switch behavior after controller disconnection. Networking guides 01–05 add no failure-mode treatment. The key needs a stated failure mode and rule-lifetime assumptions; related native material is insufficient to establish it.
question_links.review_note: State the switch failure mode and rule lifetimes. Fail-secure can continue valid forwarding entries until expiry; hybrid fail-standalone can use ordinary switching. Stale rules are a possible outcome, not a universal consequence.

evidence.section: 5.3 Practical and Algorithmic Challenges (4D / SDN)

question_links.rationale: The response-time challenge explicitly names the remote Packet-IN to Flow-MOD round trip. Initial misses can incur this delay, whereas later matching packets stay local; per-packet is misleading if read as every packet in a flow.
question_links.review_note: Use a controller round trip for an initial reactive table miss. Already installed matching rules forward later packets locally; controller intervention is not intrinsically per packet.

evidence.section: 5.3 Practical and Algorithmic Challenges (4D / SDN)

question_links.rationale: The source asks which consistency and ownership rules keep physically distributed controller decisions and switch updates compatible, including during partitions.
